'''Anne Hope Jahren''' (born September 27, 1969) is an American [[geochemist]] and [[geobiologist]] at the [[University of Louisiana at Lafayette]], known for her work using [[isotope analysis|stable isotope analysis]] to analyze [[fossil forests]] dating to the [[Eocene]]. She has won many awards in the field, including the [[James B. Macelwane Medal]] of the [[American Geophysical Union]].

Her book ''[[Lab Girl]]'' (2016) has been praised as both "a personal memoir and a paean to the natural world", a literary fusion of memoir and science writing, and "a compellingly earthy narrative".<ref name="Kirkus">{{cite news|title='Lab Girl' by Hope Jahren (review)|url=https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/hope-jahren/lab-girl/|access-date=7 March 2016|work=[[Kirkus Reviews]]|date=January 5, 2016|archive-date=March 7, == Early life and education ==
Jahren was born in [[Austin, Minnesota]], on September 27, 1969. Her father taught science at a community college and she has three older brothers.<ref name="Nautilus"/> She completed her undergraduate education in geology at the [[University of Minnesota]], graduating ''[[cum laude]]'' in 1991.<ref name=CV>{{cite web |url = http://jahrenlab.com/storage/JahrenCV09182013.pdf |title = Jahren CV |date = 18 September 2013 |access-date = 6 February 2014 |last = Jahren |first = Hope |archive-date = February 22, 2014 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222033618/http://jahrenlab.com/storage/JahrenCV09182013.pdf |url-status = live }}</ref>

== Career and research ==
Jahren earned her Ph.D. in 1996 at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in the field of [[soil science]].<ref name=CV/><ref name="thesis-jahren-1996">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/304244091/ |title=The stable isotope composition of the hackberry (Celtis) and its use as a paleoclimate indicator |date=1996 |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Jahren |first=Anne Hope |id={{ProQuest|304244091}} |url-access=subscription |oclc=931663536 |access-date=December 23, 2022 |archive-date=November 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231129160155/https://www.proquest.com/docview/304244091/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Her dissertation covered the formation of [[biomineralization|biominerals]] in plants and used novel stable isotope methods to examine the processes.<ref name=AGU/> From 1996 to 1999, she was an assistant professor at the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]], then moved to [[Johns Hopkins University]], where she stayed until 2008.<ref name=CV/>

At Georgia Tech, she conducted research on [[paleoatmosphere]]s using fossilized plants, and discovered the second [[methane hydrate]] release event that occurred 117 million years ago. She also spent a year on a [[Fulbright Award]] at the [[University of Copenhagen]], learning DNA analysis techniques.<ref name=AGU/>

While at Johns Hopkins, Jahren received media attention for her work with the fossil forests of [[Axel Heiberg Island]]. Her studies of the trees allowed her to estimate the environmental conditions on the island 45 million years ago. She and her collaborators analyzed depletion of oxygen isotopes to determine the weather patterns there that allowed large ''[[Metasequoia]]'' forests to flourish during the Eocene.<ref name=JHU/><ref name=NatGeo>{{cite journal |url = http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2002/03/0326_020326_TVredwoods.html |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20020802044805/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2002/03/0326_020326_TVredwoods.html |url-status = dead |archive-date = August 2, 2002 |journal = National Geographic Today |access-date = 6 February 2014 |last = Trivedi |first = Bijal P. |date = 26 March 2002 |title = Arctic Redwood Fossils Are Clues to Ancient Climates}}</ref><ref name=Geotimes>{{cite journal |journal = Geotimes |date = June 2002 |title = Warm winds in the Arctic |last = Lawrence |first = David |access-date = 6 February 2014 |url = http://www.geotimes.org/june02/NN_arctic.html |archive-date = April 9, 2019 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190409172138/http://www.geotimes.org/june02/NN_arctic.html |url-status = live }}</ref> Her research at Johns Hopkins also included the first extraction and analysis of DNA found in [[paleosol]] and the first discovery of stable isotopes existing in a multicellular organism's DNA.<ref name=AGU/>

In 2008, Jahren left Johns Hopkins for a full professorship at the [[University of Hawaii]].<ref name=JHU/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hope Jahren {{!}} Climate One |url=https://www.climateone.org/people/hope-jahren |access-date=2025-07-29 |website=www.climateone.org |language=en}}</ref> Her research there focused on using stable isotope analysis to determine characteristics of the environment on different timescales.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://jahrenlab.com/hope-jahren-background/ |title = Background |last = Jahren |first = Hope |access-date = 6 February 2014 |date = 2012 |archive-date = February 22, 2014 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222032718/http://jahrenlab.com/hope-jahren-background/ |url-status = live }}</ref>  On September 1, 2016, Jahren became the J. Tuzo Wilson Professor at the [[University of Oslo]]'s Centre for Earth Evolution and Dynamics, where she studies how living and fossil organisms are chemically linked to the environment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mn.uio.no/geo/english/people/aca/ceed/hope/index.html|title=Anne Hope Jahren|access-date=2016-09-01|archive-date=September 12, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160912004326/http://www.mn.uio.no/geo/english/people/aca/ceed/hope/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref> She is now an Adjunct Professor at the [[University of Louisiana at Lafayette]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-03-30 |title=Faculty & Staff |url=https://geos.louisiana.edu/about-us/faculty-staff |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=School of Geosciences |language=en}}</ref>

== Writing career ==

In addition to her research contributions, Jahren is also a writer. Her memoir "Lab Girl", published in 2016 gives perspectives on science and gender dynamics. Jahren discusses her experiences as a woman in the scientific field and reflects on the life lessons she learned during her childhood. The book encompasses topics such as gender dynamics in STEM fields, the challenges encountered by women scientists, and her personal and professional journey to success as a scientist and author. "Lab Girl" chronicles her life and career in science.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

In 2020, Jahren published "The Story of More: How We Got to Climate Change and Where to Go from Here."<ref>{{cite web |title=The Story of More How We Got to Climate Change and Where to Go from Here |url=https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/575671/the-story-of-more-by-hope-jahren/ |website=Penguin Random House |publisher=Penguin Random House |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> The book grew out of her experience teaching courses on climate change.<ref>{{cite web |title=About the Author |url=https://www.northwestern.edu/onebook/story-of-more/about/about-the-author.html |website=Northwestern |publisher=Northwestern University |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
Jahren has received three [[Fulbright Award]]s: in 1992 for geology work in Norway, in 2003 for environmental science work in Denmark, and in 2010 for arctic science work in Norway.<ref name=CV/> In 2001, Jahren won the [[Donath Medal]], awarded by the [[Geological Society of America]]. In 2005, she was awarded the Macelwane Medal, becoming the first woman and fourth scientist overall to win both the Macelwane Medal and the Donath Medal.<ref name=AGU>{{cite web |url = http://honors.agu.org/winners/a-hope-jahren/ |title = A. Hope Jahren |publisher = American Geophysical Union |date = 2013 |access-date = 7 February 2014 |last = Dove |first = Patricia |archive-date = December 4, 2013 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131204172550/http://honors.agu.org/winners/a-hope-jahren/ |url-status = live }}</ref><ref name=JHU>{{cite journal |url = http://www.jhu.edu/jhumag/0605web/science.html == Support for science awareness ==

Jahren is an advocate for raising public awareness of science and has been working to lift the stereotype surrounding [[women and girls in science]].<ref name="msnbc.com2">{{cite news|url=http://www.msnbc.com/craig-melvin/watch/a-twitter-hijack-of-manicuremonday-114901571927|title=What's the Big Idea? A twitter hijack of #ManicureMonday|date=January 12, 2014|work=MSNBC.com|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref> One such example included the repurposing of the Twitter [[hashtag]] #ManicureMondays.<ref name="hopejahrensurecanwrite.com2">{{cite web|url=http://hopejahrensurecanwrite.com/2013/11/20/what-i-learned-from-manicuremonday/|title=What I learned from #ManicureMonday|last1=Jahren|first1=Hope|website=hopejahrensurecanwrite|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140129102125/http://hopejahrensurecanwrite.com/2013/11/20/what-i-learned-from-manicuremonday/|archive-date=January 29, 2014|url-status=dead|access-date=November 20, 2013}}</ref> [[Seventeen (American magazine)|''Seventeen'' magazine]] originally came up with the hashtag, but focused mainly on manicured and painted fingernails. Subsequently, Jahren encouraged fellow scientists, specifically girls, to tweet pictures of their hands conducting scientific experiments.<ref name="msnbc.com2" /> The idea behind this was to raise awareness of scientific research and to increase the profile of women working in science.<ref name="hopejahrensurecanwrite.com2" /><ref name="O'Connor2">{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4276980/hope-jahren-lab-girl-interview/|title=Hope Jahren on Plants, Mud Manicures and Science's Woman Problem|last1=O'Connor|first1=Siobhan|date=March 31, 2016|magazine=Time|access-date=13 April 2018}}</ref>

Jahren has also written compellingly about the [[sexual harassment]] of women in science. She recommends that people draw strong [[professional boundaries]], and that they carefully document what occurs, beginning with the first occasion of harassment.<ref name="NYT2016">{{cite news|last1=Jahren|first1=A. Hope|title=She Wanted to Do Her Research. He Wanted to Talk 'Feelings.'|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/06/opinion/sunday/she-wanted-to-do-her-research-he-wanted-to-talk-feelings.html?smid=tw-nytopinion&smtyp=cur|access-date=7 March 2016|work=The New York Times|date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=March 10, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160310063902/http://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/06/opinion/sunday/she-wanted-to-do-her-research-he-wanted-to-talk-feelings.html?smid=tw-nytopinion&smtyp=cur|url-status=live}}</ref>
